content: Efforts to improve cognitive function in individuals with schizophrenia face significant challenges. However, given the broader health benefits of exercise, there is a pressing need to prioritize supervised exercise programs for this population. Studies that focused solely on yoga or tai chi were excluded from analysis, as these practices are believed to provide cognitive benefits distinct from those derived from physical activity alone. Cognitive outcomes assessed included global cognition, working memory, social cognition, and attention/vigilance, with significant improvements noted in working memory and social cognition. However, no significant effects were observed for processing speed, verbal memory, visual memory, or reasoning and problem-solving. A systematic review by Krog et al. aimed to evaluate the effects of exercise on individuals diagnosed with depression. The review included randomized clinical trials that assessed depression severity, lack of remission, and serious adverse events (e.g., suicide) at the end of the intervention. Secondary outcomes included quality of life, adverse events (e.g., injuries), and follow-up assessments of depression severity and remission rates. The review analyzed 35 trials involving 2,498 participants. Results indicated no significant antidepressant effects of exercise in trials with lower risk of bias. Additionally, exercise did not significantly impact quality of life, depression severity, or remission rates during follow-up. Data on serious adverse events and injuries were insufficient to draw conclusions. A meta-review by Stubbs et al. examined the benefits of physical activity (PA) across severe mental illnesses (SMI), including schizophrenia-spectrum disorders, major depressive disorder (MDD), and bipolar disorder. The review highlighted that PA can improve depressive symptoms in MDD, with effects comparable to antidepressants and psychotherapy. PA also enhanced cardiorespiratory fitness and quality of life in MDD, though its impact on physical health outcomes was limited. Larger effects were observed when PA was delivered at moderate-to-vigorous intensity and supervised by exercise specialists. For schizophrenia-spectrum disorders, aerobic PA was shown to reduce psychiatric symptoms, improve cognition and its subdomains, and enhance cardiorespiratory fitness. Research on PA in bipolar disorder was limited, preventing definitive recommendations. No cost-effectiveness analyses were identified for PA interventions in any SMI condition. The review emphasized the need for further research to address existing gaps and to integrate PA into routine clinical care to improve psychiatric and medical outcomes. Mind-body interventions, such as yoga and tai chi, were excluded from the analysis. Outcomes addressed included neuropsychological test performance, depression severity, remission rates, and adverse events.
